}}'''Alastair Ian Scott''' (10 April 1928 in [[Glasgow]] – 18 April 2007) was a British-American [[organic chemist]] who achieved international renown for elucidating the biosynthetic pathway of [[vitamin B12]].<ref name=Obit/>

He occupied successive chairs of organic chemistry at the universities of [[University of British Columbia|British Columbia]], [[University of Sussex|Sussex]], and [[Yale]] before moving to [[Texas A&M University]] in 1977.<ref name=UoI/> In 1980 he occupied the Forbes Chair of Organic Chemistry at the [[University of Edinburgh]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ourhistory.is.ed.ac.uk/index.php/Chemistry#Forbes_Chair_of_Organic_Chemistry|title=Chemistry - Our History|website=ourhistory.is.ed.ac.uk}}</ref> He was named a distinguished professor of chemistry and biochemistry in 1981 at Texas A&M University, and remained there until the end of his career.<ref name=Obit/>

In 1964 he won the [[Corday-Morgan Medal]] of the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]] (RSC). He was awarded the 1975 [[Ernest Guenther Award]] and the 1994 Arthur C. Cope Scholar Award by the [[American Chemical Society]] (ACS). He gave the [[Centenary Prize|RSC Centenary Lecture]] in 1994 and the [[Royal Society]] [[Bakerian Lecture]] in 1996. He took the [[Tetrahedron Prize]] (1995), the RSC Natural Products Award (1996), the [[Welch Award in Chemistry]] (2000),<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.welch1.org/Awards/WelchAwardinChemist0943/PreviousRecipients.asp|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110930041332/http://www.welch1.org/Awards/WelchAwardinChemist0943/PreviousRecipients.asp|url-status=dead|archive-date=30 September 2011|title=Previous Recipients|date=30 September 2011|accessdate=26 March 2019}}</ref> the [[Royal Society]]'s [[Davy Medal]] (2001), the Queen's Royal Medal of the [[Royal Society of Edinburgh]] (2001), and the ACS [[Nakanishi Prize]] (2003). He was Texas Scientist of the Year in 2002.<ref name=Obit>{{cite web| url=http://www.science.tamu.edu/news/2007/04/texas-am-mourns-loss-of-distinguished-chemist-ian-scott/| title=Texas A&M Mourns Loss of Distinguished Chemist Ian Scott| date=19 April 2007| website=Science.tamu.edu| access-date=22 October 2018}}</ref><ref name=UoI/>

He was a Fellow of the Royal Society and the Royal Society of Edinburgh, the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] and the European Academy of Sciences.<ref name=UoI>{{cite web|url=https://chemistry.illinois.edu/events/lectures/Nelson_J_Leonard_Distinguished_Lecturers/Alastair_Scott.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170504223523/https://chemistry.illinois.edu/events/lectures/Nelson_J_Leonard_Distinguished_Lecturers/Alastair_Scott.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=4 May 2017|title=Alastair Ian Scott / Chemistry at Illinois|date=4 May 2017|accessdate=26 March 2019}}</ref> In addition, he was an honorary member of the Japanese Pharmacological Society.<ref name=Obit/>

==Personal life==
Alastair Ian Scott married Elizabeth Wilson Walters at the [[University of Glasgow Memorial Chapel]], on 4 March 1950. They had two children: Anne and William.
Alastair died in Texas on 18 April 2007, following a heart attack. He was survived by his wife, two children and six grandchildren.<ref>{{Cite web|title= Alastair Ian Scott 10.4.1928 to 18 April 2007|website=University of Sussex Biographical Archive Chemistry|url= http://www.sussex.ac.uk/suss-ex/ChemBiographies.pdf|accessdate=11 December 2023}}</ref>
Elizabeth died at her home in [[Grapevine, Texas]] on 13 September 2016, aged 89.<ref>{{Cite news|title= Elizabeth Wilson Scott, 89, passed away Tuesday, Sept. 13, 2016, at her home in Grapevine|newspaper= Fort Worth Star-Telegram|location=Fort Worth|date=23 September 2016}}</ref>
